summary:
Space Sibü is a digital health monitoring platform designed to support human well-being during space missions and in remote environments on Earth.

The platform aims to integrate physiological monitoring, mental health support, physical training, and medical information into a unified, intuitive experience.

Through interactive dashboards and a human-body visualization, users can explore health indicators, identify potential concerns, and better understand their physical and psychological condition.

Space Sibü is designed with a modular architecture that supports future integration with wearable devices, health data sources, and intelligent monitoring systems.

Our vision is to make health monitoring more accessible, proactive, and understandable, helping individuals and mission-support teams make informed decisions in environments where timely medical assistance may be limited.
details:
What it does and how it works

Space Sibü is a browser-based health monitoring platform with two views. In the Crew view, astronauts check their current status, mark any area on an interactive body map to log a symptom, and review their history. They also complete mood check-ins, use guided breathing and cognitive-behavioral exercises, follow a weekly training plan, map their support network, and send delayed messages to family on Earth. In the Physician view, the flight surgeon sees every reading and entry each astronaut records, including vital-sign trends, biomarker references, a layered 3D anatomy viewer, medical case and inventory tools, and mission-environment data for the ISS, Moon, Mars, or transit. An emergency protocol assigns roles and a step-by-step checklist to the whole crew.

Under the hood, vitals can come from a scenario, a live simulation, an imported CSV or FHIR file, or a Bluetooth heart-rate monitor. Each reading is compared with the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline. Our analytics module then uses recent trends (3- and 7-day windows) to predict, seven days ahead, the risk of the problems astronauts may face, such as cardiovascular, bone, sleep, behavioral, and renal issues. It issues three alert levels (nominal, caution, early warning) and explains which factors drove each one. The AI only analyzes recorded data and predicts; it generates nothing.

Benefits

  • Gathers body, mind, and relationships in one place, so astronauts can evaluate their own status and act without waiting for Earth.
  • Personalizes every comparison to the individual, not to a population average.
  • Turns data into early warnings with clear reasons, not black-box scores.
  • Gives the physician a complete picture for remote support.

Intended impact

We want to make autonomous health care practical for long-duration missions, where distance, isolation, radiation, and altered gravity put bones, hearts, immune function, and mental health at risk. By helping astronauts catch changes early and act on them, Space Sibü supports safer, more self-reliant missions on the way to Mars.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, WebXR, and MediaPipe for on-device camera framing.
  • Backend: Python 3.14, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, PostgreSQL 18, and a versioned OpenAPI contract.
  • Analytics: pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn (logistic regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Isolation Forest, PCA), and SHAP for explainability.
  • Quality: pytest, Vitest, mypy, ruff, oxlint, and oxfmt, with 576 backend and 169 frontend tests.
  • Hardware: none required beyond a browser on the habitat’s local network. An optional Bluetooth heart-rate monitor is supported.
  • Reference data: values and thresholds drawn from NASA technical sources and published spaceflight research.

What makes it creative

  • A cockpit-style interface with function keys and system keys, so the app feels like part of the spacecraft.
  • A body map that lets astronauts point to where something feels wrong instead of filling out forms.
  • A single platform that treats mental health, family connection, and relaxation (Earth soundscapes, circadian lighting) as core health indicators next to vital signs.
  • Predictions personalized to each astronaut’s own baseline and evaluated with grouped cross-validation, so the model is tested on astronauts it never saw during training.
  • A “portable core” mode that works with or without the expansion module.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delay: messages show their delay and are queued, never hidden.
  • Data integrity: every reading shows its source and timestamp, and missing values are shown as “No data,” never filled in.
  • Explainability: every alert says why it fired.
  • Accessibility: color-blind palette, keyboard shortcuts, reduced-motion support, and a mobile layout.
  • Safety: a deliberate two-step emergency activation to avoid accidental triggers.
  • Maintainability: modular code and documented architecture decisions so sensors and new data sources can be added later.
